t: Binary File Analyzer: a plain-language overview
title: Binary File Analyzer: a plain-language overview
description: Overview: what the Binary File Analyzer does and why archives need it. A binary file analyzer looks at a file's raw bytes instead of its name. Files usually begin with a signature — a few magic bytes like the PNG header — that says what kind of file it really is. By reading those signatures and measuring how random the bytes look, the analyzer can identify, sort, and describe files even when their names are wrong or missing.
demo:
# Binary File Analyzer - runnable demo (JAH-ATK152-000001)
import math
from collections import Counter
RANK = 1
SIG = False
SAMPLE = bytes.fromhex('89504e470d0a1a0a0000000d49484452')
MAGIC = {b"89504e470d0a1a0a": "PNG image", b"7f454c46": "ELF executable",
         b"4d5a": "PE/DOS executable", b"504b0304": "ZIP archive", b"25504446": "PDF document"}
def entropy(data):
    if not data: return 0.0
    c = Counter(data); n = len(data)
    return -sum((v/n) * math.log2(v/n) for v in c.values())
kind = "unknown"
for sig, name in MAGIC.items():
    if SAMPLE.startswith(sig):
        kind = name; break
print("size:", len(SAMPLE), "bytes")
print("identification:", kind)
print("shannon entropy: %.2f bits/byte" % entropy(SAMPLE))
if RANK >= 2:
    text = "".join(chr(b) if 32 <= b < 127 else "." for b in SAMPLE[:64])
    print("ascii preview:", text)
if RANK >= 3:
    halves = [entropy(SAMPLE[i:i+32]) for i in range(0, len(SAMPLE), 32) if SAMPLE[i:i+32]]
    print("entropy by 32-byte block:", ["%.2f" % h for h in halves])
if SIG:
    print("Signature lineage stamp: JAH-SIG-BIN-" + "JAH-ATK152-000001")
print("record:", "JAH-ATK152-000001", "OK")

t: How the Binary File Analyzer works: the deep tour
title: How the Binary File Analyzer works: the deep tour
description: Overview: what the Binary File Analyzer does and why archives need it. Real analyzers compare the first bytes of a file against a signature database (the libmagic database behind the Unix file command holds thousands of patterns), then parse known container structures: ELF and PE headers for executables, chunk layouts for PNG, or ZIP central directories. Shannon entropy separates compressed or encrypted regions (high entropy) from code or text (lower entropy), and printable-string extraction surfaces embedded messages, paths, and version banners. The output is an identification plus a structural sketch of the file. Advanced analysis disassembles executable sections to list imported functions, walks archive members without extracting them, and carves known structures out of damaged disk images by their headers and footers. Accuracy is checked against corpora of labeled binaries; the hard limits are packed or obfuscated executables, where the true structure is deliberately hidden, and proprietary formats with no public specification. Analyzers therefore report confidence and mark regions they could not interpret rather than guessing.

title: Using the Binary File Analyzer every day
description: Production: how the Binary File Analyzer runs at archive scale and plugs into the extraction pipeline. A binary file analyzer looks at a file's raw bytes instead of its name. Files usually begin with a signature — a few magic bytes like the PNG header — that says what kind of file it really is. By reading those signatures and measuring how random the bytes look, the analyzer can identify, sort, and describe files even when their names are wrong or missing.
demo:
# Binary File Analyzer - runnable demo (JAH-ATK152-000013)
import math
from collections import Counter
RANK = 1
SIG = False
SAMPLE = bytes.fromhex('89504e470d0a1a0a0000000d49484452')
MAGIC = {b"89504e470d0a1a0a": "PNG image", b"7f454c46": "ELF executable",
         b"4d5a": "PE/DOS executable", b"504b0304": "ZIP archive", b"25504446": "PDF document"}
def entropy(data):
    if not data: return 0.0
    c = Counter(data); n = len(data)
    return -sum((v/n) * math.log2(v/n) for v in c.values())
kind = "unknown"
for sig, name in MAGIC.items():
    if SAMPLE.startswith(sig):
        kind = name; break
print("size:", len(SAMPLE), "bytes")
print("identification:", kind)
print("shannon entropy: %.2f bits/byte" % entropy(SAMPLE))
if RANK >= 2:
    text = "".join(chr(b) if 32 <= b < 127 else "." for b in SAMPLE[:64])
    print("ascii preview:", text)
if RANK >= 3:
    halves = [entropy(SAMPLE[i:i+32]) for i in range(0, len(SAMPLE), 32) if SAMPLE[i:i+32]]
    print("entropy by 32-byte block:", ["%.2f" % h for h in halves])
if SIG:
    print("Signature lineage stamp: JAH-SIG-BIN-" + "JAH-ATK152-000013")
print("record:", "JAH-ATK152-000013", "OK")

title: The Binary File Analyzer in production
description: Production: how the Binary File Analyzer runs at archive scale and plugs into the extraction pipeline. Real analyzers compare the first bytes of a file against a signature database (the libmagic database behind the Unix file command holds thousands of patterns), then parse known container structures: ELF and PE headers for executables, chunk layouts for PNG, or ZIP central directories. Shannon entropy separates compressed or encrypted regions (high entropy) from code or text (lower entropy), and printable-string extraction surfaces embedded messages, paths, and version banners. The output is an identification plus a structural sketch of the file.

t: The Binary File Analyzer at archive scale
title: The Binary File Analyzer at archive scale
description: Production: how the Binary File Analyzer runs at archive scale and plugs into the extraction pipeline. Real analyzers compare the first bytes of a file against a signature database (the libmagic database behind the Unix file command holds thousands of patterns), then parse known container structures: ELF and PE headers for executables, chunk layouts for PNG, or ZIP central directories. Shannon entropy separates compressed or encrypted regions (high entropy) from code or text (lower entropy), and printable-string extraction surfaces embedded messages, paths, and version banners. The output is an identification plus a structural sketch of the file. Advanced analysis disassembles executable sections to list imported functions, walks archive members without extracting them, and carves known structures out of damaged disk images by their headers and footers. Accuracy is checked against corpora of labeled binaries; the hard limits are packed or obfuscated executables, where the true structure is deliberately hidden, and proprietary formats with no public specification. Analyzers therefore report confidence and mark regions they could not interpret rather than guessing.
